sections.name: The Doctor Who Told Everyone to Wash Their Hands

lines.prompt: A crowded 1840s Vienna hospital ward with rows of beds, worried mothers holding newborn babies, gaslight

lines: In 1840s Vienna, women giving birth in hospital were dying of a deadly fever.

lines.prompt: A doctor in a dark coat walking from a dissection room straight into a maternity ward, his hands dirty, no blood visible

lines: A young doctor, Ignaz Semmelweis, noticed something. Doctors were coming straight from autopsies to deliver babies.

lines.prompt: Close-up of hands scrubbing in a basin of cloudy chlorine water, a doctor watching proudly

lines: In 1847, he made them wash their hands in chlorinated lime first.

lines.prompt: The doctor holding up a chart with a line dropping sharply, nurses smiling, bright window

lines: Deaths on his ward dropped dramatically.

lines.prompt: A group of older 1840s doctors in top hats laughing and turning away from the young doctor

lines: But many doctors were offended by the idea that their own hands were spreading disease.

lines.prompt: A modern nurse washing hands at a sink with soap foam under bright hospital lights, a poster of handwashing steps behind

lines: Semmelweis died in 1865, mostly ignored. Today he's called the saviour of mothers.
